# Chat Input Scope

## Concept

### Pitch

A multi-line, syntax-highlighted textbox that accepts plain text as well as snippets of Piton.

### Shape

#### Description

Input on the left, send button on the right.
<Enter> allows for creating new lines, like Ctrl/Cmd+Enter sends it to the HarnessIntegrationScope
Sending is never blocked by the harness working: while it is, the send button on the Code, Chain, and Spec tabs reads "Queue" and sending adds the prompt to prompt mode's queue. On the Ask tab it always reads "Send", because a question is never queued. The button is only disabled while the input is empty.

#### Tabs

##### Overview

The input and send button live inside the body of a tab bar, using gpui-kit's default tab styling. There are four tabs, in order: Code, Chain, Spec, and Ask. Code, Spec, and Ask are ordinary tabs. Chain is also a tab, just a small one, because it only shows an icon. All four sit flush against each other with no extra gaps, and no tab has more padding than a normal tab.
Pressing <Tab> while in the chat input cycles from Code to Chain to Spec to Ask and back to Code, <Shift+Tab> the other way, and focus remains in the chat input.

##### Chain

Chain is a tab with unusual behaviour. It shows an icon rather than a label, reading "Code and Spec" as its tooltip, and selecting it selects both Code and Spec. It never shows a focus outline, and its icon looks evenly spaced between Code and Spec whichever of the two is selected.
Unselected, it shows a broken chain dimmed to 50% opacity, and sits between Code and Spec like any other tab, overlapping neither of them.
Selected, it shows a joined chain at full opacity. Selecting it animates as though it took a margin of -50% of its own width on both its left and right sides: Code and Spec slide together until they meet underneath it, so it ends up sitting on top of both. Deselecting it animates them apart again. While Chain is selected, Code and Spec both show as selected and read as a single unified tab, with no line between them. Chain itself has a transparent background and no left or right borders, so the joined Code and Spec show through underneath it.

##### Help

To the right of the tabs, filling the rest of the bar, a line of help text says what the selected tab is for, and changes as soon as another tab is selected. It is extra small and dimmer than muted text, set a little apart from the last tab, so it reads as a quiet note about the tab rather than as another tab. It is cut off rather than wrapped when the bar is too narrow.

###### Code

Changes the code, leaving the spec as it is.

###### Chain

Changes the code and the spec together.

###### Spec

Changes the spec, leaving the code as it is.

###### Ask

Asks a question about the code and the spec, changing neither.

##### Colour

The selected tab and the tab body holding the input are tinted: a subtle red for Code, a subtle blue for Spec, and a subtle green for Ask. With Chain selected, Code, Spec, and the body are all purple. The colour transitions smoothly whenever the selected tab changes, straight from the old tab's colour to the new one's. The tabs wrap around, so pressing <Tab> on Ask fades green straight to Code's red, and <Shift+Tab> on Code fades red straight to Ask's green; neither lights up Chain or Spec on the way.

#### System Prompt

The selected tab is the mode a prompt is sent in, and each mode gives the hidden anchor a systemPrompt property alongside its userPrompt. The code location is `codeRoot` and the spec location is `root`, as set in the project's piton.config.pi.

##### Code

We're working on the code located in <code location>. Don't edit the spec located in <spec location>.

##### Spec

We're working on the spec located in <spec location>. Don't edit the code located in <code location>.

##### Both

We're working on both the code located in <code location> and the spec located in <spec location>. Edit both of them.

##### Ask

We're only asking a question about the code located in <code location> and the spec located in <spec location>. Don't edit either of them.

These are the defaults; each is saved with the project and can be edited in the [SettingsWindowScope](../../settings-window/SettingsWindowScope.md).
A prompt keeps the mode it was sent in while it waits in the queue.

#### Ask

Ask is for simply asking a question. A question runs straight away, separately from any Code, Chain, or Spec task, even while the harness is working on one. Any number of questions can be asked, and they all run at the same time; asking another never stops or waits for one already running.
Each question's progress and results are shown in a task table, as in the [MessageList](../message-list/MessageList.md). The questions stack directly above the tabs, the newest nearest them, in a column that pushes the message list up to make room rather than covering it, so none of a running task's progress is ever hidden behind them. Each slides up out of the chat input with an animation as it is asked, the message list giving way above it. While the harness works on a question, it is a single row showing the latest thing the harness did. A finished question is a row with its status and first line.
Once a question is complete, it opens onto a heading, with its status and first line, above its full task table, in the answer drawer, which it fills, scrolling once it is taller, with a [ScrollbarScope](../../../ui/components/scrollbar/ScrollbarScope.md) and its lock to the bottom. Only one question is open at a time: opening another closes the one open back down to its row. An open question leaves the stack for the drawer. Clicking an open question's heading closes it down to its row in the stack, and clicking a finished question's row opens it again. Each question has a close button, which removes it and stops it if it is still running, leaving the others running. A closed question becomes a previous answer.

#### Answer Steps

For a question, only the answer matters, so the steps leading up to it are collapsed by default wherever a finished question's task table is shown: an open question, and a previous answer. The steps are every row up to and including the harness's last tool call; the answer is the rows after it. In their place, the table's first row reads "Show 1 step" or "Show N steps", muted, beside a right chevron, with the answer beneath it. A single click on that row expands the steps in place, above the answer, and the row then reads "Hide 1 step" or "Hide N steps" beside a down chevron; clicking it again collapses them. Each question's table is expanded or collapsed on its own, and a question closed into the previous answers starts collapsed again.
A reply with no tool calls, or with nothing after its last one, has nothing to collapse and shows whole. A question still running shows its latest step as usual. Tasks are never collapsed like this, since their whole chain is of interest: see the [MessageList](../message-list/MessageList.md).

#### Previous Answers

Previous answers are a [HistoryListScope](../../../ui/components/history-list/HistoryListScope.md), shown only while the Ask tab is selected, at the top of the questions stacked above the tabs. It lists every question asked before and closed: those saved with the project and those closed since. Its row reads "No previous answers", "1 previous answer", or "N previous answers", and while expanded, "Back to the questions". Expanded, the row and the list go into the answer drawer, the list sliding up from on top of any question rows still in the stack, rather than out of the chat input over them: those rows stay where they were, in view and undimmed, beneath the drawer, and with no rows left there it slides up out of the chat input as usual. The questions asked from now on carry on the conversation the latest of them left off.

#### Answer Drawer

Only a question open onto its task table, or the previous answers expanded, are a drawer. Unlike the stack of question rows, which pushes what is above it, the drawer slides up out of the chat input over everything above it, the message list, any file beside it, and the stack, covering them rather than pushing them, and dims them: see the [MessageList](../message-list/MessageList.md). The previous answers are the exception: they slide up from on top of the question rows in the stack, leaving those rows uncovered and undimmed, and the drawer's share of the space counts from the chat input, rows included. Closing it slides nothing back; the stack and the message list are where they were beneath it.
The drawer opens to 80% of the height of the space above the chat input by default: the open question's table, or the previous answers list, grows to fill whatever the drawer's other rows leave, rather than stopping at a fixed height. It slides up out of the chat input as it opens.
While open, the drawer is resizable by dragging its top edge, which shows a resize cursor and a thin highlight when hovered. It follows the pointer exactly, with no slide, and can be dragged from 20% to 95% of that space. The size it is dragged to is kept for as long as the application runs, for every question or list opened afterwards, rather than going back to 80%.

#### Selecting Answer Text

The text of an answer being viewed, in the answer drawer, whether an open question or a previous answer, can be selected by dragging across it, as any text can. When a drag that selects text ends within the drawer, a small popover appears just below and to the right of where the pointer was let go, floating above everything, with two small buttons side by side: "Copy", with a copy icon, and "Attach to prompt", with a paperclip icon.
Copy puts the selected text on the clipboard. Attach to prompt adds it to the prompt as an attachment. Either one closes the popover and clears the selection. The popover also closes without doing anything when the mouse is pressed anywhere outside it, including to start selecting something else, or when the drawer closes.

#### Attachments

What is attached to the prompt is listed above the text input, between the tabs and the input, one row per attachment in the order they were attached, and only while there is anything attached. An attached piece of text shows a quote icon, the text's first line cut off with an ellipsis, and, when it runs to more than one line, how many lines it has, muted, and at the right end a small button with a cross, whose tooltip says it removes the attachment, which removes just that one.
Attachments belong to the prompt being written, not to a tab: switching tabs keeps them all, and they go with the prompt whichever tab it is sent from. When the prompt is sent, its attachments are sent along with it and the list empties, as the text input does. A queued prompt keeps the attachments it was sent with.

#### Escape

Pressing <Escape> while in the chat input takes focus out of the chat input.

#### Grow To Fit

The text input will grow to fit the text inside of it, one row per visual line: both lines broken with <Enter> and long lines that soft wrap. It shrinks again as text is removed, and re-fits when the window is resized. It starts at a single row, lined up with the send button, and stops growing at 12 rows, after which it scrolls.

#### Auto Focus

The chat input should be auto-focused.

#### Syntax Highlighting

Syntax highlighting will be supported via the [Tree Sitter Grammar](https://github.com/piton-lang/tree-sitter-piton)

#### Lsp

[LSP](../../lsp/LSP.md)

#### Harness Mentions

```
overview: Typing `/` offers the harness's skills and commands, and typing `@` offers its agents, the way they are offered in the harness itself. The placeholder mentions both.
trigger: A mention starts at `/` or `@` at the start of the input or after whitespace, so paths and email addresses never open it, and an at sign followed by an opening curly brace is still a Piton reference. Completions are requested after typing the `/` or `@`, and after each letter, digit, hyphen, underscore, or colon of the name that follows. Only inside a mention are a slash or a hyphen a trigger; outside of one they never reach the [LSP](../../lsp/LSP.md).
offered: Skills and commands are those of the selected ProjectDirectoryScope, of the user, and of the user's enabled plugins, a plugin's own being named `plugin:name`. Agents come from the same places, plus the harness's built-in agents. Each shows whether it is a skill, command, or agent, and its description as documentation when it has one. Every harness run reports the skills and agents it has, built-in ones included; the last report is saved with the project and offered too. Results are narrowed and ordered like Piton completions: matches at the start of a name before matches anywhere in it, then by name.
accepting: Accepting a skill or command inserts `/name `, and accepting an agent inserts `@agent-name `, which the harness understands as a request to use that agent. They pass through the hidden anchor and its compilation unchanged, so a prompt starting with `/name` runs that skill or command. Mentions work without the [LSP](../../lsp/LSP.md).
```

#### Hidden Anchor

While the user will be able to type plain text, behind the scenes, they'll be typing into a randomly-named piton anchor with a userPrompt property.  It's this compiled anchor that will be send to the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../../harness-integration/HarnessIntegrationScope.md)

##### Attached Text

A prompt with attached text gives the hidden anchor an attachedText property: a list with an item per attached piece of text, in the order they were attached. Since attached text is taken as it is, not as Piton, each item is itself a list of the text's lines, each a quoted string, with quotes and backslashes escaped, so nothing in it is interpolated or evaluated. A prompt with nothing attached has no attachedText property.
What the harness receives is the compiled userPrompt followed by the attached text: a line reading "Attached text:", then each piece as a fenced code block, whose fence is longer than any run of backticks in the text itself. This is also the compiled prompt shown in the task's header.

Links in this document point at reference files. Read one when the work touches what it describes.

content.text:
I'd move mode switching off plain <kbd>Tab</kbd>. It's quick, but a mode switch is too consequential and too easy to trigger by accident for the most-pressed key in a text box.

**What happens now:** <kbd>Tab</kbd> and <kbd>Shift+Tab</kbd> always cycle Code → Chain → Spec → Ask. The only exception is when the completion menu is open, which keeps its own <kbd>Tab</kbd> (`cycle_tab`, `src/chat_input.rs:480`). The input catches the editor's indent and outdent actions to do this (`src/chat_input.rs:797`).

**Problems with plain Tab**
1. **You can't indent.** The input takes Piton snippets, and Piton is indentation-sensitive. Nested properties, lists and code blocks in a prompt all need indentation, and right now you have to type the spaces by hand.
2. **Mistakes are costly.** The mode decides what the agent is allowed to change: Ask changes nothing, while Code, Chain or Spec edit files. An accidental press silently turns a question into an editing task, and the colour change is the only warning.
3. **Completion habits cause misfires.** You'll often press <kbd>Tab</kbd> expecting to accept a completion that isn't open yet or has just closed, and switch mode instead.
4. **Cycling is slow.** Going from Code to Ask takes three presses through Chain and Spec, or remembering to go backwards.

**What I'd do instead**
- **<kbd>Tab</kbd>:** indent, and accept a completion when the menu is open. <kbd>Shift+Tab</kbd> would outdent only in a multi-line block. That's what users expect from a text box that takes code.
- **<kbd>Alt+1</kbd>–<kbd>Alt+4</kbd>:** jump straight to Code, Chain, Spec or Ask, with no cycling and no dependence on the current mode. Show the shortcut in each tab's tooltip.
- **<kbd>Shift+Tab</kbd> on a single line:** cycle modes. Claude Code uses <kbd>Shift+Tab</kbd> to cycle its own modes, so it's already familiar, and outdenting a single line isn't needed. Leave this out if you want <kbd>Shift+Tab</kbd> to always outdent.

A smaller change would be to keep <kbd>Tab</kbd> as the switcher only while the input is empty. That fixes indenting, but you'd still switch modes by accident right after sending.

If you go ahead, two places in `spec/scope/prompt-mode/chat-input/index.pi` need changing:
- **Tabs overview:** the Tab/Shift+Tab cycling sentence (around line 42).
- **Colour section:** the wrap-around example, which describes the tint moving when you press <kbd>Tab</kbd> on Ask (around line 94). That animation still makes sense for <kbd>Shift+Tab</kbd> cycling. Direct shortcuts would need the tint to go the shorter way round, which `move_tint` already does.
